10404-man-size:
William MacLeod Raine published this western novel in 1922, dedicating it to Captain Sir Cecil Denny of the first riders who carried law into Canada's lone lands. Raine, author of The Big-Town Round Up, writes of scarlet jackets as a synonym for justice, integrity, and pluck. The book praises the mounted police and the frontier they tamed.

Chapters move from a danger zone and an Amazon to wolfers, a man in a scarlet jacket, and trouble at Sweet Water Creek. Angus McRae does his duty, Morse jumps up trouble, and Tom makes a collection. Readers get a brisk, heroic western of law, loyalty, and the open plains.
1157-damaged-goods-the-great-play-les-av:
Upton Sinclair turns Eugène Brieux's French play into a novel. Its hero is a young man who, through ignorance and shame, contracts syphilis. He must then face what it means for his marriage and his child. The story follows his doctor, his wife, and his family as the truth comes out.

Sinclair wrote to break the silence around venereal disease, arguing that plain talk and honest medicine beat moral panic. The book shocked its day and served the public-health cause. Read now, it is both a melodrama and a document of early sex education.
17117-an-elegy-on-the-glory-of-her-sex-m:
Oliver Goldsmith's comic elegy for Mrs. Mary Blaize, pictured by R. Caldecott, praises a lady in lines that undo themselves at each turn. Good people lament Madam Blaize, who never wanted a good word from those who spoke her praise. The needy found her kind, yet always left a pledge behind, and she never followed wicked ways unless she was sinning.

Each stanza pairs a virtue with a sly catch, and Caldecott's pictures play the same game in image form. The joke is gentle: a mock elegy for a glory built on gossip and show. Young readers and verse lovers will enjoy a short, witty classic that turns praise into punchline.
21377-to-win-or-to-die-a-tale-of-the-klo:
Chapter one of George Manville Fenn's Klondike tale finds a man shouting at an echo. His voice bounces off a huge snow cliff, and he half laughs to keep from going mad in the silence. Tough men in the gold country fight for survival against cold, hunger, and each other, since robbery waits beside every trail. The title states the terms plainly.

Fenn keeps the book short and breathless, each chapter trading one desperate plight for the next without pause. The Klondike gold craze of the late 1890s drew thousands north on the same gamble. His heroes dig, freeze, and fight through it, in a tale meant to entertain by other men's misfortunes, as Fenn's transcriber honestly admitted.
21653-the-eurhythmics-of-jaques-dalcroze:
The Eurhythmics of Jaques-Dalcroze, issued at Boston in 1915, explains a new way of training through rhythm. In Germany the method went by the name of rhythmic gymnastics. The book warns that the term is too narrow for Dalcroze's wider principle.

A line from Plato fronts the work: the whole of life needs right rhythm and harmony. Dalcroze held his find was no mere polish for dancing or music teaching. It was a principle, he claimed, that must touch every part of life. Teachers of music and movement get here the method's own account of its aims and drills.
23337-tight-squeeze:
Dean C. Ing wrote this short science fiction tale, first printed in Astounding Science Fiction in the mid nineteen fifties. A spaceman knows the theory of repairing his device well enough, but practice means threading a wire through a too-small hole in zero gravity, wearing a spacesuit.

The story opens on a loading ramp, where MacNamara savors dry, dusty air before the hard job begins. Ing's tale is a neat problem story: skill, patience, and nerve against a tiny task in a hostile place. Ruiz makes radio contact with the doughnut while Mac traces leads to a small turbine-driven auxiliary motor.
23370-the-battle-and-the-breeze:
R. M. Ballantyne built this boys' sea tale around the Battle of the Nile, where Admiral Nelson's fleet beat the French. Bill Bowls, a kind and modest seaman known as Fighting Bill, stands at its heart, with his mates Ben Bolter and Tom Riggles close beside him.

The book opens on Bill's boyhood, so unlike the bronzed, whiskered sailor he becomes, then moves to ship life, action, and the bonds of a crew at war. Ballantyne mixes plain facts of naval fighting with human scenes of courage, humour, and loss. Young readers get a brisk war story that also shows how ordinary sailors lived, worked, and stood by each other under fire.
28461-the-combined-maze:
May Sinclair's The Combined Maze, published in February 1913, opens above a run-down chemist's shop on Wandsworth High Street in the early 1880s. There John Randall Fulleymore Ransome, called Ranny, is born to Fulleymore Ransome, a weedy, furtively drinking chemist, and his wife Emma.

Ranny grows into a furniture dealer's clerk, confined in a long mahogany pen making invoices for chairs and tables. Yet he also leads Section I at the London Polytechnic gymnasium, dreaming of cleanness, health, and physical perfection. Sinclair's novel follows his long battle against flabbiness and weediness, and the maze of lives his ambition entangles.
32347-time-fuze:
Randall Garrett's story, illustrated by Paul Orban, follows the first vessel ever to leave the Solar System into disaster. The cover line says the ultradrive carried one small flaw: its shock wave blew suns apart, so reaching home turned tricky. Commander Benedict watches the rear plate while he switches on the intercom and orders the power cut.

Dr. Leicher, of the staff, calls the position safe, although even this far off, a nova would make a display. He notes the light will not reach them for hours, since they outran it at ten lights. Benedict calls it the worst coincidence that could strike the first vessel ever to leave the Solar System. Leicher adds that they will never learn if Alpha Centauri A ever held planets. Readers get a space story of a nova, a shock wave, and a delicate return.
32531-deepfreeze:
Robert Donald Locke's tale, printed in Imagination in January 1953, follows Edwin Dollard, the last of America's industrial tycoons, fleeing Earth in its death agony. Dollard, nervous fingers spilling Scotch from a fifth highball, turns from horrors on a telescreen as Garth enters by a panelled tunnel door. Garth reports the ship ready in two hours and adds that the men still know nothing, since he slipped them poison at noon mess.

Dollard relaxes at the thought that only he and Garth will survive, calling the others stupid sheep fit to die, and dreaming of plague-untouched women on Venus. Garth agrees it will feel like rebirth, while Dollard snaps that he remains boss. Locke's title points to the cold bargain at the story's heart: survival bought by betrayal, with a last laugh still to come.
6023-catharine-furze:
Mark Rutherford, in the voice of Reuben Shapcott's edition, opens on a bright, hot August Saturday in 1840 in Eastthorpe, an ancient market town in the eastern Midlands. The town lies five miles west of the Fens, level country on a broad, deep river that barely falls enough to reach the sea.

A six-arched stone bridge, a High Street, and narrower streets joined by courts and alleys shape the place, with an immense church at its center, famed for spire and eight bells. Around the churchyard live the doctor, lawyer, parson, and two aged gentlewomen. Catharine Furze grows from this provincial ground.
6569-bessie-bradford-s-prize:
Joanna Mathews returns to Bessie Bradford in the third sequel to her Bessie books, with a prize at stake and a household full of talk. The chapters move from a policeman's house and a bundle of letters to a secret, a stolen mail scare, and a box of bonbons. Friends, kin, and young rivals crowd the scenes, each with a claim on Bessie's time.

At the heart of the tale sits a trust that must be kept, a charge that must be faced, and the plain question of who wins in the end. Mathews writes for young readers in a warm, direct voice, with manners and morals woven into daily fun. Bessie Bradford's Prize is a gentle girls' story of honesty tried under small but real pressure.
7899-the-radio-boys-first-wireless-or-wi:
Allen Chapman's The Radio Boys' First Wireless, or Winning the Ferberton Prize, opens with a foreword by Jack Binns on radio's storm across America. Boy amateurs, he says, have already advanced the young science, and E. H. Armstrong began at home in Yonkers with homemade gear.

Armstrong's circuit, Binns notes, made broadcast music and speech possible, and a boy today may still win honor and reward by experiment. An illustration shows Joe crying out as music bursts on their ears. The tale follows boy builders chasing a prize with sets, signals, and pluck.
an-elegy-on-the-glory-of-her-sex-mrs-mar: Oliver Goldsmith writes an elegy on the glory of her sex, Mrs. Mary Blaize, pictured by Randolph Caldecott for his picture books. The comic verses praise a lady whose virtues are told with tongue firmly in cheek. Printed by Edmund Evans, the little book pairs Goldsmith's wit with Caldecott's art.
bessie-bradford-s-prize:
Joanna H. Mathews's Bessie Bradford's Prize is the third sequel to her Bessie books, a girls' story built around a contest and its unexpected turns. Bessie and her friends move through a round of visits, letters and small mysteries, with a policeman's house, a box of bonbons and a stolen-mail scare among the episodes.

Chapters titled Lena's Secret, Robbing the Mail, A Confidence, Discovery and Accusation carry the plot toward the question of the final chapter: who wins? Mathews dedicates the book to her young friend Elizabeth Leiper Martin, herself a fellow author, and W. St. John Harper provides the illustrations. The story suits readers who enjoy gentle Victorian tales of friendship, honesty and schoolgirl society.
britannica-1911-baize:
Baize is a cloth first named, probably, for its colour. The French word baies hints at bay colouring. Another guess links it to Avignon berries. Such berries may once have dyed the cloth. Baize is usually a coarse woollen fabric. It carries a long nap, or raised surface.

The cloth is commonly dyed green or red. Cotton versions are made now too. Refugees brought its making to England. They came from France and the Netherlands. That arrival fell in the 16th century. Baize serves chiefly for curtains and linings. Lighter makes sometimes serve for clothing. Table baize is a kind of oilcloth. It covers tables cheaply and cleans easily.
britannica-1911-belize:
Belize, also written Balize, is the capital and chief seaport of British Honduras, on the Caribbean Sea. It stands on both banks of the river Belize at its mouth and counted 9,969 people in 1904. Wooden houses with high roofs and wide verandahs, shaded by palms, make up most of the town.

Court house, government house, Fort George and the Wesleyan church are its main buildings, while mangrove swamps round it breed fevers. Belize ships out mahogany, rosewood, cedar, logwood, sugar and bananas, and takes in breadstuffs, cloth and hardware. Its name may come from the French balise, a beacon lit for buccaneers, or from a Scottish settler called Wallis.
britannica-1911-blaze: Blaze is a short word study in the 1911 Britannica, from an Old English word for a torch. Its first sense is a fire or bright flame. A second sense gives the white mark on a horse or cow's face, tied to a German word for pale white. American use adds the mark cut into bark to show a path. A verb sense, to blaze abroad, comes from an Old English verb meaning to blow. The entry ends by noting a muddle with blazon.
britannica-1911-bonze: Bonze is the European name for Buddhist monks and priests in Japan and China, and the entry is a single short paragraph. The word comes from the Japanese bonzo. That in turn is thought to be a mispronunciation of a Chinese term, fan sung, meaning a religious person. The name is also used loosely, the entry adds, for all Buddhist priests in those lands and in the countries near them.
britannica-1911-breeze:
Breeze carries two quite apart senses, and the entry keeps them apart. First it names a light current of air, weaker than a plain wind and far weaker than a gale. The word is tied most closely to the sea-breeze that blows inland by day and the land-breeze that blows out to sea at night.

Word history fills much of the piece. French brise, Spanish brisa and kindred forms point to a north or north-east wind. English first used the term for the cool east or north-east wind of the West Indies and the Atlantic coast of Central America. The second sense is wholly apart: fine ash and cinder left from coal, coke and charcoal fires, traced to an old French word for embers.
britannica-1911-bronze:
Bronze is an alloy formed wholly or chiefly of copper and tin in varying shares. The word has been linked to the same root as brown. Berthelot is cited for a place-name source: aes Brundusianum, Brundisian copper, with Pliny noting Brundisian mirrors of tin and copper mixed as the best known to earlier ages.

Adding tin to copper makes a metal that melts more easily and casts better, and that is harder and less malleable than copper alone. A soft bronze or gun-metal takes 16 parts of copper to 1 of tin, and a harder gun-metal for bronze cannon about doubles the tin. Uchatius's steel bronze used 8 per cent tin, hardened further by cold rolling. Bronze at about 7 parts copper to 1 of tin is hard, brittle and sonorous and can be tempered to a fine edge, while bell-metal varies widely in its mix.
britannica-1911-fuze:
Fuze, or fuse, is the appliance used for firing explosives in blasting and in military shells. Military engineers have settled on the spelling with a z, to keep this sense apart from melting by heat. The word is traced to the Latin fusus, a spindle, since the ordinary fuze takes a spindle-like tube shape. The same root gives the fusee of watch trains, a coned spindle that evens out the pull of the mainspring, and the fusil of heraldry, an elongated lozenge.

In electrical work a fuse, always spelled with an s, is a strip or wire of easily melted metal set in a circuit. When accident makes the current too strong, the metal melts and breaks the circuit before harm is done. This second sense ties the word to fusus as the past participle of fundere, to pour.
britannica-1911-gauze:
Gauze, in the 1911 Britannica, is a light, open-woven fabric, first of silk and later also of linen or cotton. It is said to take its name from Gaza in Palestine, where it was first made. Some eastern gauzes, the entry notes, were brocaded with gold or silver flowers.

The weaving is the heart of the piece. Warp threads are twisted in pairs after each pass of the weft, which holds the weft threads evenly spaced and parallel. The entry covers plain, striped and figured gauzes, and the cotton form called leno. It recalls the silk-gauze trade of western Scotland, strong in the later 1700s and then much declined. Uses run from dress to sifting flour, and the name extends to fine wire cloth in safety lamps and sieves.
britannica-1911-houffalize: Houffalize is a small town high up, nearly 1,100 ft., in the far south-east of the Belgian province of Luxemburg. Summer visitors come for its fine, bracing air. It holds the ruins of an old castle and remains of the still older abbey of Val Ste Catherine. Its parish church dates from the 13th or 14th century. Inside are two old black marble tombs, to Thierry of Houffalize and to Henri his son, killed at Woeringen in 1288. The town stands on the eastern Ourthe. Its population was 1,486 in 1904.
catharine-furze:
Catharine Furze, by Mark Rutherford, opens in Eastthorpe, a market town, on a hot August Saturday in 1840. Rutherford was the pen name of William Hale White. He surveys the town slowly. A six arched stone bridge crosses a broad river. An immense church lifts a famous spire and eight bells. In the Abbey Close, the doctor, the lawyer, and the parson live in old red brick houses. Long gardens run behind them.

This printing, from Hodder and Stoughton in 1913, belongs with his Eastthorpe sequence, the same world as Clara Hopgood. Catharine Furze grows up inside that watched town. The novel follows her through family duty and religious feeling. It follows the claims of a love the town would not choose for her. White writes provincial life as moral weather: nothing dramatic on the horizon, and everything at stake in the climate of a single household.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-baluz:
Etienne Baluze was a French scholar and historian, born at Tulle on 24 December 1630 and dead in Paris on 28 July 1718. His education began at the Jesuit college of his native town, where he distinguished himself by intelligence, constant devotion to study, and prodigious memory. On his professors' recommendation he won a scholarship to the College of Saint Martial at Toulouse, founded by Pope Innocent VI for twenty Limousin students.

Resolved to study literature and history, Baluze worked with great zeal, perseverance, and success. Critical and painstaking, he studied French origins, customs, laws, and institutions from genuine documents and original records, not fanciful legends, introducing a scientific spirit into historical research. At twenty-two he wrote a remarkable work of historical criticism. Father Frizon, a Jesuit, had just published Gallia purpurata, lives of the French cardinals, which succeeded greatly until Baluze's Anti-Frizonius of 1652 corrected many of its errors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Greuze, a French painter born at Tournus in 1725 and dead in Paris in 1805, won fame overnight with scenes of home life. His father, a master tiler, meant him for building. Instead he sent him to Lyons to learn painting, and in 1755 he reached Paris with a picture of a father reading the Bible to his children.

The Academy took him at once, and the picture's success made him famous in a day at thirty. Italy, visited late in 1755, left little mark on him; he soon returned to humble and middle-class subjects, painted with feeling and moral warmth. That vein brought a long run of success, though later taste turned and his last years were less kind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theophile-jul:
French chemist Théophile-Jules Pelouze, pharmacist turned professor and mint chief, is the man of science traced here. Born at Valognes on 26 February 1807, he died at Paris on 31 May or 1 June 1867. He learned pharmacy at La Fère, went to Paris in 1827 as assistant to Gay-Lussac, and worked for a time at La Salpêtrière hospital before quitting for research.

Lille made him professor in 1830, the Mint made him assayer in 1833, and the Polytechnic School took him on staff. Collège de France kept him as professor till 1851. Germany in 1836 brought joint work with Liebig on organic chemistry, and the Academy of Sciences took him in 1837. Mint Commission president in 1848 and Paris Municipal Commission member in 1849, he resigned public posts in 1852.
damaged-goods-the-great-play-les-avarie-:
Upton Sinclair novelized Eugene Brieux's play Les Avaries as Damaged Goods, with the French dramatist's approval and a handwritten letter from Brieux in the front matter. Sinclair's preface says he took the play to pieces and rebuilt it as a novel, keeping Brieux's dialogue word for word where possible. The New York Times called the play's production epoch-making.

The story follows Georges Dupont, who contracts syphilis before marriage, hides it, and infects his wife and child; doctors and family then fight over blame and silence. Brieux and Sinclair meant to break the conspiracy of shame around venereal disease. The frankness shocked American audiences and made the work a landmark of social-problem drama.
doe-osti-2588881-challenges-in-quantifyi: Burying nuclear waste forever got its doubt measured, and this DOE report tackles the unknown unknowns. The pages detail the repository math. The geologists get their briefing. The burial was deep. The unknowns were unknown. The math was repository. The report was DOE's.
doe-osti-3001981-development-of-crown-et: Lithium capture got crown ether sorbents, and this DOE report develops the polymeric materials. The pages detail the findings. The battery folks get their method. The capture was lithium-ion. The method was battery. The materials were detailed. The method was capture.
man-size:
Man-Size is a Western novel by William MacLeod Raine, dated 1922. Raine dedicated it to Captain Sir Cecil Denny of the Mounted Police. He honors the first riders who carried law into the lone lands. Scarlet and gold, he says, stood for justice and pluck.

The contents open in the danger zone, with a woman called the Amazon. Angus McRae does his duty among wolf-hunters and bad men. A man in a scarlet jacket rides through the tale. Sweet Water Creek and camp-fire talk fill out the frontier world. Raine sets this adventure on the Canadian plains. It is hearty, swift Western fiction of the old school.
nasa-tm-19670012747-unusual-resonance-li:
Uri Feldman and Leonard Cohen, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, report a spectroscopic puzzle in this paper. While studying the spectra of highly ionized atoms, they found weak lines that matched no expected transitions. The lines sat in a region that should have been empty.

For a given element, the lines fell in an energy gap. The gap lies above the ionization potential in one electron sequence and below the first excited state in another. Such lines are easy to spot when the expected spectrum is simple. The authors lay out the case, including the two transitions possible from the first excited configuration.
podcast-dannyjones-vcgJXirykZE:
Former CIA officer John Kiriakou and writer Matthew Cox break down the assassination attempt on Donald Trump for Danny Jones. Kiriakou brings an intelligence insider's eye to the shooting and the security failure around it. Cox, a former fugitive, adds a criminal's read of the official story.

The pair go through the timeline, the rooftop, and the questions that still linger. Kiriakou judges the Secret Service performance with professional disbelief. Jones steers them through the theories without losing the known facts. Watching and skeptical listeners get an insider's analysis of a day that nearly changed history.
podcast-joerogan-cUwd-D94pzE:
Longevity scholar David Sinclair joins Joe Rogan to tell how fasting can help fight aging in a segment from the show. Sinclair is the Harvard name in youth science. His tips reach far past the lab in this cut.

Sinclair explains why gaps in food intake wake the body's repair crews, as his work reads them. He lays out fast plans a normal man can try, from skipped meals to long gaps. Rogan asks what he does in his own week. Listeners get a tight, useful cut from their longer talks. The library holds the segment as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-nqbRepVizzE:
Episode 179 of the Joe Rogan Experience brings Duncan Trussell back in the show's early days. Trussell, a comic with a mystical streak, was already becoming a fan favorite. The young podcast was still loose and small, and this talk shows that raw feel.

Trussell rambles through love, death, God, and the cosmos in his warm, funny style. Rogan laughs along and steers him back when the ideas drift too far out. Between the jokes sit real moments about grief and meaning. Early listeners can hear the bond that made Trussell one of the show's defining repeat guests.
podcast-tuckercarlson-vKBOrkk1FZE:
Mike Benz joins Tucker Carlson to explain the arrest of Telegram founder Pavel Durov in France. Benz argues the arrest was really about forcing control over one of the last big platforms resisting state pressure. The free-speech fight, in his telling, has gone global.

Benz lays out the deep state's plan, as he calls it, to bring encrypted and open platforms to heel. He connects the Durov case to his wider map of censorship programs. Carlson asks what tools governments will use next against private speech. Wary and wired viewers get a critical briefing on the fight for the internet.
the-battle-and-the-breeze:
R. M. Ballantyne's sea story, dated 1869, follows Bill Bowls, called Fighting Bill, from babyhood to life on a man-of-war. Chapter one calls him gentle, kindly, and modest, yet lion-hearted. As a child he loved water, swam early, and feared almost nothing.

Bill recalls launching a plank at about four years old, sailing it, and being wrecked in a squall before his millwright father pulled him out. Later he worked in the coasting trade, survived wrecks, and sailed for China under a tyrant captain. Storms, typhoons, and disaster marked his career, yet he kept turning up alive and cheerful.
the-radio-boys-first-wireless-or-winning:
Allen Chapman's boys' novel opens with a foreword by Jack Binns praising radio at the moment it has taken the country by storm. Binns argues that amateurs, often boys with homemade sets, have driven key advances in the young science.

His example is E. H. Armstrong of Yonkers, whose boyhood experiments led to the circuit that made broadcast music and speech possible. Secretary of Commerce Herbert Hoover is quoted in support of the American boy experimenter. The story that follows, about winning the Ferberton Prize, is thus framed as encouragement for young builders to persist against odds.
